findings.summary: A benchmark code block from the performance chapter is dropped onto the definition page, using four identifiers that are never introduced and illustrating nothing on that page.
findings.evidence: Page 1 block: `func BenchmarkIface(b *testing.B) { var s Shape = rect{2, 3}; for range b.N { sink = s.Area() } }` — `Shape`, `rect`, `sink` and the whole benchmarking/dispatch-cost topic appear nowhere on page 1, whose sections are "A Set Of Signatures", "Behaviour, Not Data", "The Empty Set" and "Nil Has Two Words".
findings.fix: Delete the block from page 1 and move it to the costs/performance page (syllabus ch.9, "Benchmark shape: `func BenchmarkIface(b *testing.B)` comparing a direct call, an interface call, and a generic call"), where `Shape`/`rect` can be declared alongside it.

findings.summary: The caption promises ten pages but the carousel has only seven titled pages.
findings.evidence: Caption: "Ten pages of field notes: implicit satisfaction, the method-set rule, iface/eface internals, embedding, type switches, and the ten gotchas worth memorising." — titles array contains 7 entries ("What an Interface Actually Is" … "Promotion Rules & Type Assertions").
findings.fix: Change "Ten pages of field notes" to "Seven pages of field notes" (or drop the count: "Field notes on:") so the caption matches the deck length.

findings.summary: The counting-writer method body appears on page 2 while the `cw` struct it belongs to — and the embedding that makes `c.Writer` legal — are only introduced on page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 2: `func (c *cw) Write(b []byte) (int, error) { c.n += len(b); return c.Writer.Write(b) // delegate }` vs. page 7 "Decorator In Six Lines": `type cw struct { io.Writer; n int }`.
findings.fix: Move the `Write` method block to page 7 directly under the `type cw struct` declaration so the decorator is shown whole, and replace it on page 2 with an example that actually demonstrates structural typing (e.g. a non-struct named type satisfying an interface).

findings.summary: A section states the embedding-promotion rules using "embed" and "promote" as known terms, two pages before embedding and promotion are defined.
findings.evidence: Page 4, "Embedding Obeys It Too": "Embed `T` in `S`: value methods promote to `S` and `*S`" — promotion is first explained on page 6: "Promotion generates a forwarding method, not inheritance".
findings.fix: Move this two-bullet section to page 6/7, appending it to the promotion discussion as "promotion follows the same method-set rules", rather than stating it before the reader knows what embedding is.

findings.summary: The rule for when storing a value in an interface allocates is stated as a size test, but Go boxes every non-pointer-shaped value regardless of whether it fits in a word.
findings.evidence: "If it does not fit a pointer word it is heap-allocated first" — immediately followed by "Since Go 1.4 the data word is always a real pointer", which contradicts it. An `int` fits in a pointer word yet `convT64` still boxes it (allocating, or pointing into `runtime.staticuint64s` for values < 256).
findings.fix: Replace with the shape test: "Only pointer-shaped types (pointer, map, chan, func, single-pointer struct) are stored directly; everything else — including an `int` that would fit — is boxed and usually heap-allocated."

findings.summary: Three bullets describe itab construction, caching and dispatch before the itab is defined, and the list has no stated subject.
findings.evidence: Page 5 bullets: "Built once per (interface, concrete type) pair", "Cached in a global hash table", "`w.Write(b)` = load `tab.fun[i]`, indirect call with `data`" — but the itab's contents are only shown on page 6 ("Inside The itab": inter / _type / hash / fun[0..n]).
findings.fix: Move the "Inside The itab" diagram from page 6 to page 5, immediately before these bullets, and give the list a lead-in heading such as "The itab" so "Built once per…" has an antecedent and `tab.fun[i]` is already defined.

findings.summary: The dispatch-cost section makes a claim about type assertions before assertions are introduced on page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 6, "Dispatch Speed": "Assertions compare the stored type pointer or hash — cheap, not free" — the two assertion forms are first shown on page 7 ("Two Assertion Forms": `s := i.(string)` / `s, ok := i.(string)`).
findings.fix: Drop that bullet from page 6 and place the assertion-cost claim on page 7 after the comma-ok form has been shown, or on the later costs page.

findings.summary: The caption promises ten pages and coverage of type switches, but the part has seven slides and never mentions type switches.
findings.evidence: "Ten pages of field notes: implicit satisfaction, the method-set rule, iface/eface internals, embedding, type switches, and the ten gotchas worth memorising." — the `slides` array contains 7 entries, and no slide contains a `switch x := i.(type)` construct or the words "type switch".
findings.fix: Change to "Seven pages" and drop "type switches" from the list (or add a type-switch slide), and drop "the ten gotchas" unless a numbered gotcha list is actually present.

findings.summary: "A named set of method signatures — nothing else" is no longer accurate for Go 1.18+, where interfaces may also contain type elements.
findings.evidence: "A named set of method signatures — nothing else" on a page that elsewhere cites Go 1.18 ("`any` is an alias for it since Go 1.18"). Since 1.18 an interface may embed type elements — unions and `~T` approximations — e.g. `interface{ ~int | ~string }`.
findings.fix: Qualify it: "A set of method signatures — plus, since Go 1.18, optional type elements (`~int | ~string`) usable only as generic constraints."

findings.summary: The stdlib table lists `io.Reader`'s method without its results, contradicting the deck's own rule that results are part of the signature.
findings.evidence: Table row "`io.Reader`" → "`Read([]byte)`", while the same page states "Signature = name + parameter types + result types" and page 3 states "One differing parameter or result means no satisfaction". The real method is `Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)`.

findings.summary: Page 1 explains the nil interface and interface satisfaction in vocabulary that pages 3 and 5 are the ones to define.
findings.evidence: Page 1: "It holds any concrete value whose method set fits" and "Type word and data word both unset" — but "method set" is defined on page 3 ("The methods callable on a value of a given type") and the two-word layout on page 5 ("Two Words Wide… interface value, 16B on 64-bit").
findings.fix: On page 1, either phrase these as "whose methods include those signatures" and "a nil interface records neither a type nor a value", or add one line to the nil callout stating that an interface value is a (type, data) pair, forward-referencing page 5.

findings.summary: The closing flow diagram hinges on consumer-defined interfaces, a placement rule not introduced until page 2.
findings.evidence: Page 1 diagram nodes: ["concrete type", "consumer's interface", "assignment", "compile check"]; page 2 is where the idea first appears: "The consumer package declares it, so producers import nothing".
findings.fix: Relabel the page 1 node as plain "interface type" (the diagram's point there is where satisfaction is checked), and keep "consumer's interface" for a diagram on page 2.

findings.summary: The claim that `*T` satisfies strictly more interfaces than `T` is false for types with no pointer-receiver methods.
findings.evidence: "`*T` satisfies strictly more interfaces than `T`" — but if every method of `T` has a value receiver, the two method sets are identical, so the inclusion is not strict.
findings.fix: Change to "`*T` satisfies at least as many interfaces as `T`, and strictly more as soon as one method has a pointer receiver."

findings.summary: Sealing via unexported methods is overstated: outside packages can satisfy a sealed interface by embedding it.
findings.evidence: "Unexported methods seal an interface, e.g. `testing.TB`" / "Only the declaring package can satisfy a sealed one" — `struct{ testing.TB }` in any package satisfies `testing.TB`, because the unexported `private()` method is promoted.
findings.fix: Add the escape hatch: "…unless you embed the interface itself, which promotes the unexported method — this is how test-helper wrappers around `testing.TB` work."

findings.summary: The escape-analysis command block sits under a slices-and-maps heading and uses `iface` and heap-escape cost, both of which are only explained on page 5.
findings.evidence: Page 4, under "Slices And Maps Fool You": `go build -gcflags=-m ./...` / `# moved to heap: c  <- escaped into an iface`, while page 5 supplies "Pointer copies one word but may push the value to the heap" and the definition "Non-empty: `iface{ tab *itab, data unsafe.Pointer }`".
findings.fix: Move the `-gcflags=-m` block to page 5, placing it directly after the "may push the value to the heap" bullet, and spell the comment as "escaped into an interface" since `iface` is introduced on that same page.

findings.summary: The append gotcha is asserted on page 4 with no example, while the code that demonstrates it lands on page 5 beneath an unrelated heading about copying locks.
findings.evidence: Page 4: "`append` updates only the local slice header" / "The caller keeps seeing the old length" (no code); page 5, under "Copying Locks": `func (b Buf) Add(x int) { b.s = append(b.s, x) } // caller's len(b.s) unchanged`.
findings.fix: Move the `Buf.Add`/`Add2` code block to page 4 directly under the "Slices And Maps Fool You" bullets so the claim and its demonstration sit together, leaving "Copying Locks" to the mutex material.

findings.summary: In the "Inside The itab" diagram, connector lines are drawn on top of node boxes so they strike through the node labels.
findings.evidence: The node labelled "type hash" has a vertical connector running down between "type" and "hash", and the edge descending from "fun[0..n]" crosses the "concrete type" box rather than terminating at its border.
findings.fix: Route the diagram edges around node boxes (or draw nodes above edges with an opaque fill) so no connector passes over "interface type", "concrete type", or "type hash".

findings.summary: In the "Name Resolution" diagram, a connector line passes through the "shadows, wins" node instead of stopping at its edge.
findings.evidence: The vertical edge coming down from "depth 1" continues across the "shadows, wins" box, cutting through the word "shadows" on its way to "promoted".
findings.fix: Clip diagram edges at node boundaries (or give nodes an opaque background and a higher z-order) so the "shadows, wins" label is not crossed.
